Coupes budgétaires dans la francisation: Budget Cuts to Francization: A New Barrier for Immigrants
Quelques semaines avant la rentrée scola: A few weeks before the start of the school year, the province announced budget cuts affecting adult francization programs.

A few weeks before the start of the school year, Quebec’s Ministry of Education announced budget cuts affecting francization programs for adults. What surprised me most, and what shocked thousands of francization students and teachers, was how quickly the consequences of these measures were felt.
Des étudiants qui s’apprêtaient à commen: Students who were about to start francization classes learned at the last minute that there would be no space for them after all. The luckier ones were redirected to other classes, but the schedules didn’t necessarily work for them.
De plus, le ministère de l’Immigration,: On top of that, the ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration (MIFI) announced an imminent end to allowances for all part-time students.
À la lecture de ces nouvelles, je n’ai p: Reading this news, I couldn’t help thinking of the government’s latest measures freezing work permits. Once again, these measures were mainly affecting immigrants. To me, these budget cuts were another way for the government to signal that it no longer wanted the very immigrants it had welcomed itself.
C’est par ailleurs un rapport que Camill: That is also the connection Camille Caron Belzil, one of the two francization teachers I interviewed, made right away. “You hear more and more that immigrants are partly responsible for housing problems, as if they were the cause of all ills... But I didn’t think it would go as far as cuts to francization,” she told me.
Pour ce reportage, ce qui a été le plus: For this report, the hardest part for me was finding students affected by these measures. Not because there are few of them, but because the community organizations that offer francization classes are funded by the MIFI. There are confidentiality clauses. Dozens of community organizations refused to speak to me, and even to point me toward students outside their structure. In the end, one organization, whose name I will withhold, opened its doors to me. Two students, whose testimonies are heart-wrenching, shared their reality with us, and I’ll let you discover it.
Bonne lecture et à très vite !: Happy reading, and see you soon!
Quelques semaines avant la rentrée scola: A few weeks before the start of the school year, the Quebec Ministry of Education (MEQ) announced budget cuts affecting francization programs for adults. These measures are raising concerns about immigrant integration, as immigrants once again see their learning of French compromised. A report.
Le gouvernement québécois offre gratuite: The Quebec government offers free French classes to residents aged 16 and over. These classes are meant to ease immigrants’ integration by giving them language skills. Yet a recent change to financial assistance has sent a chill through those who depend on it. Several classes have been cut or reduced, despite growing demand. The final blow came last September 23, with the suspension of the $28 daily allowances for part-time students. The $230-a-week compensation for full-time classes, however, has been maintained. In addition, employees of companies with 100 or more workers no longer receive the allowance for workplace francization.
<strong>« Le gouvernement ne pense pas à: “The government doesn’t think about students’ real lives”
Ces changements ont des répercussions po: These changes have repercussions for thousands of people. That’s the case for Sandra* and Pryia*, two women who now find themselves at an impasse. We meet them in the offices of a community organization that offers MIFI-funded francization classes.
Sandra, petite de taille, a les cheveux: Sandra, small in stature, has her hair tied back, which gives her a solemn air. A Colombian immigrant, she arrived alone in Montréal in September 2023. I meet her as she comes out of class, in an office at the organization. Sandra stares at the empty tables and opens up. “I chose Canada for its safety, and Quebec specifically because I wanted to learn French. I had started classes with a teacher in Colombia, but once I got here, it was something else: the accent, the expressions…” says the woman in her thirties, laughing.
Dès son arrivée, Sandra a cherché à s’in: As soon as she arrived, Sandra tried to register for francization classes. But because the system was saturated, it was nearly a year later, last August, that a spot opened up at an organization, though it was an hour and forty-five minutes away from her home by transit. “When I arrived, I was living in Lachine, so I applied there. But I never got an answer. I had time to move twice, to Pie-IX, then to Jean-Talon, before they called to tell me there was finally a spot. For weeks, I made long round trips every day… I was determined.” In the end, she was transferred to a centre closer to home, a relief, she tells us.
« En Colombie, j’ai étudié la littératur: “In Colombia, I studied literature, I was a Spanish teacher and a writer. But here, as long as I don’t speak French well, I’m condemned to low-paying odd jobs,” she says, referring to the string of jobs she’s had to take as a cleaner or a hostess. “My savings were melting away, so honestly, starting French classes also relieved me financially, because I was receiving the allowances. I thought it would make my life a little easier.”
Puis viennent les annonces des coupes bu: Then came the announcements of the budget cuts, which upended everything. For Sandra, it’s a hard blow: “I already don’t buy my groceries at the supermarket, I can’t afford it. I go to the food bank. These allowances help me pay for my room and my $100-a-month Opus card. I don’t even know how I’m going to renew it next month,” she says, her voice trembling. “For now, I bike, but with winter coming, that won’t be possible anymore…”
Et, avec une pointe d’ironie, elle ajout: And, with a hint of irony, she adds: “Having the chance to learn French for free is incredible, but when I think about those parents who also have to find a way to feed their children… I don’t have kids, unfortunately, but at the same time, thank God, I’m not a mother!”
À quelques mètres de là, à l’extérieur d: A few metres away, outside the classroom, Pryia, another student, shares this feeling of helplessness. A mother of three children aged nine, five and two, originally from India, Pryia stands out for her easy smile. With her glasses resting on her head, her floral but understated top and her orange-toned lipstick, she suggests a personality that is both lively and serious. Her eyes light up as she recounts her arrival in Canada three years ago as an asylum seeker. After obtaining her citizenship, she started francization classes. “These allowances helped me be a little independent from my husband. I’m here every day, for a total of 20 hours of class a week. Even though I wasn’t working, I had the satisfaction of having my own money,” she says.
Ancienne administratrice en Inde, Pryia: A former administrator in India, Pryia already speaks four languages and is determined to master French. She laughs as she recalls her beginnings: “When I got here, I didn’t even know the French alphabet! Now I want to keep learning so I can help my children. They already speak French fluently, but I still have to persevere.”
Cependant, pour elle, la possibilité de: However, for her, the option of switching to full-time classes to receive the $230-a-week compensation doesn’t seem realistic. Pryia is categorical: “With three children, it’s impossible for me. Part-time was an excellent compromise. I’ll keep learning the language, especially for my children. But I know many women in my situation are going to give up francization classes to go to work… it’s a shame!” she says.
Sandra est elle aussi prise entre deux f: Sandra, too, is caught between a rock and a hard place. In November, she will start full-time digital marketing studies at an English-language college. The young woman had hoped to keep receiving the $28-a-day compensation so she could combine her marketing studies with French classes. “I’m creative, I know I can do many things, but it’s a question of survival. Of course, I want to keep learning French, but I need to work to live with dignity,” she says, aware of the need to prioritize her college studies and find a job.
Malgré les défis, les deux femmes ne per: Despite the challenges, both women are not losing hope. One thing is clear to them, however: the reality of francization students sometimes seems far removed from the decisions made by the government. “[It] doesn’t think about students’ real lives,” Sandra concludes, with a hint of disillusionment in her voice.
Ces dernières semaines, plusieurs Centre: In recent weeks, several school service centres (CSS) have been forced to drastically reduce their course offerings following budget cuts by the Quebec Ministry of Education (MEQ).
Deux semaines après la rentrée, Lisa*, p: Two weeks after the start of the school year, Lisa*, a francization teacher at the English Montreal School Board, saw her class disappear. “Classes started on August 26, and the students had already organized their whole lives around their schedule and the fact that they would be paid. Everything was turned upside down in a few days,” she laments. It would have been more “respectful,” she thinks, to let the students finish the year. “Letting them continue until 2024 would have given them time to adapt, instead of changing everything right after the start of the school year!” she says with a hint of irritation.
Certains étudiants ont été redirigés ver: Some students were redirected to part-time classes with different schedules, and the majority to full-time classes, which still entitle them to allowances. “Many went to full-time, but you have to understand that the initial choice of part-time wasn’t trivial,” she points out.
Camille Caron Belzil, également professe: Camille Caron Belzil, also a francization teacher, still can’t believe it: “I was very surprised, really very surprised. Maybe I’m a bit out of touch.” For her, these cuts come in a context where critical rhetoric toward immigrants is growing. “You hear more and more that immigrants are partly responsible for housing problems, as if they were the cause of all ills... But I didn’t think it would go as far as cuts to francization,” she says regretfully.
Cette rhétorique « xénophobe<em> »</em>,: This “xenophobic” rhetoric, according to Camille, seems to justify reducing French classes, as if these workers were seen as a financial burden. “It feels like they cost us a lot. If Quebec truly valued immigrants, decisions like these wouldn’t be made,” she concludes, visibly dismayed.
De 2019 à 2024, le financement alloué au: From 2019 to 2024, funding allocated to school service centres for adult francization rose from $69 million to $104 million. A sum that doesn’t impress the teacher, who is more concerned about the human impact. “These services meet real needs. Beyond simple economic calculations, francization classes also have a humanitarian dimension,” replies Camille Caron Belzil.
Elle rappelle que de nombreux élèves son: She points out that many students are asylum seekers fleeing oppressive regimes and trying to rebuild their lives. For her, it is the government’s responsibility to ensure access to these classes. “Without this training, they find themselves trapped in underpaid, low-skilled jobs, with no possibility of improving their situation. Maybe that’s part of the government’s calculation…”
La suppression des allocations quotidien: The elimination of the $28 daily allowances for part-time students only worsens this situation. “They are anxious, torn between the urgency of earning money to support their families and the need to learn French so they can hope for a better future,” she explains. Without this financial aid, many have no choice but to prioritize work, even if it compromises their integration.
Lors d’une entrevue accordée au <em>Devo: In an interview with Le Devoir on September 13, the Minister of the French Language, Jean-François Roberge, stated: “Instead of using Francisation Québec’s money to give out allowances, we are going to invest directly in francization classes. That way, we will be able to fulfill our mandate more effectively by francizing a greater number of people.” According to the minister, the allowances were meant to encourage newcomers to sign up for French classes. However, following the surge in registrations last spring, the CAQ government deemed this assistance superfluous. Also according to figures obtained by Le Devoir, in April and May in Quebec, the number of adults registered in francization classes reached 26,656, compared with 34,060 for all of 2023-2024.
De retour à l’organisme, Sandra, les mai: Back at the organization, Sandra, hands clasped, still has her gaze fixed on the empty tables. Like Camille, she sees these measures as relentless persecution of those who chose Quebec to build a new life. “I didn’t come here illegally. I got a study permit, I followed all the rules. It was hard, but going back to my country wasn’t an option. So I followed the government’s rules to stay here,” she insists, indignant.
Bien que consciente des priorités nation: Although aware of national priorities, Sandra deplores the stigmatization she feels she is subjected to: “I understand that Canada has to think of its citizens first, but we are educated professionals. We have a lot to give to this society. Now, they’re putting up a new barrier. We live here too! Our goal isn’t to stay home waiting for allowances. Those who receive this assistance, like refugees, are also looking for opportunities to integrate better.”
Elle marque une pause, puis ajoute, sur: She pauses, then adds, in a more bitter tone: “What they’re doing now is an act of ill will toward us. I can understand if they don’t want to help those who haven’t arrived in the territory yet, but for those who are already here, who work and try to be useful to this society, it’s simply not fair to impose these conditions on us. The message we’re getting is that they don’t want us to actually be part of this society!” exclaims the francization student.
Au moment d’écrire ces lignes, le MIFI n: At the time of writing, the MIFI had not responded to questions put to it by La Converse.
Alors que les coupes budgétaires freinen: While the budget cuts are significantly hampering immigrant integration, francization teacher Lisa stresses that these reductions also compromise students’ future prospects in Quebec. “Many of them need to obtain their francization certificate to access the Quebec Selection Certificate (CSQ), a key step toward obtaining permanent residency,” she points out.
